## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f11-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Carbon in, CO₂ out</dt><dd>Every tonne of carbon burned makes 3.67 t of CO₂: a tonne of oil makes 3.19 t, gas 2.69 t and coal 2.44 t.</dd>
<dt>Compare by heat</dt><dd>Per MWh of fuel heat coal sends 341 kg of CO₂ and gas 202 kg; per MWh of useful heat or electricity, the equipment's efficiency comes in too.</dd>
<dt>Leaks count too</dt><dd>A 2.3% leak adds about 0.70 t of CO₂e to a tonne of gas over 100 years.</dd>
<dt>Pollutants can be caught</dt><dd>Controls cut coal's SO₂ from 38 to 3.8 kg a tonne; no control on this page touches its CO₂.</dd>
<dt>Burden, not bill</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-burden">Energy burden</span> is home energy spending divided by income: Prairie City's lowest-income group spends less than the highest, yet its representative household carries 14.9% against 1.9%.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Gross and net heat, and why coal varies per tonne</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Net heat.** The IPCC counts the [net calorific value]{.lx-term term="net-calorific-value"}: the heat a fuel gives, leaving out the heat in the water vapor it forms.
- **Gross heat** is about 5% higher than net for coal and oil, and about 10% higher for most natural gas.
- **Gross-heat sources.** EPA's AP-42 and EIA count gross heat, so their CO₂ per unit of heat is a little lower than the IPCC's for the same fuel.
- **Coal types vary much more per tonne than per unit of heat.** Sub-bituminous coal holds 18.9 GJ a tonne: 1.82 t of CO₂ a tonne, yet 346 kg per MWh of heat, close to bituminous coal's 341.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Methane over 100 years or 20</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A [global warming potential]{.lx-term term="global-warming-potential"} (GWP)** compares the warming from a tonne of a gas with a tonne of CO₂ over a chosen horizon.
- **Fossil methane's 29.8** over 100 years includes the CO₂ it finally turns into; the GHG Protocol uses it for leaks from oil and gas systems.
- **The horizon is a value choice.** Methane breaks down within decades while CO₂ stays far longer, so a 20-year horizon counts methane much more: say which you use.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The spreading toy, as a formula</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Winds from every direction carry the particles out through ever wider rings while rain and the ground remove them. From $r_0$ = 10 km out, each person at distance $r$ (km) breathes, relative to the dose at $r_0$,

$$c(r) = \frac{r_0}{r}\, e^{-(r - r_0)/L}, \qquad \text{share within } R = 1 - e^{-(R - r_0)/L}$$

- $L$ = 300 km is the toy's illustrative reach; people live evenly around the plant, so the people in a ring grow with $r$ while each one's dose falls.
- **At 100 km:** $c$ = 7.4% of the dose at 10 km, and 74% of the toy's exposure beyond 10 km happens farther out.
- **Inside 10 km** the toy says nothing: there a tall stack's plume may not yet have reached the ground.
- **Real estimates** use air-quality models with real winds, chemistry and where people live: EPA's benefit-per-ton values come from such models across the continental United States.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Work the numbers yourself</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Carbon to CO₂.</b> Burning 2 t of carbon makes 2 × 44 ÷ 12 = 7.33 t of CO₂: each carbon atom joins two oxygen atoms from the air, so 12 mass units of carbon become 44 of CO₂.</li>
<li><b>A 2% leak.</b> The leak is a share of all the gas produced, so 0.02 ÷ 0.98 = 0.0204 t of methane escapes per tonne burned, × 29.8 = 0.608 t of CO₂e.</li>
<li><b>Short tons.</b> EPA's $57,000 is per short ton of SO₂ (907.18 kg), so 38 kg is 38 ÷ 907.18 × 57,000 = $2,388, in 2019 dollars.</li>
<li><b>Next.</b> Which CO₂ number answers which question, with emission factors: <a href="a10-emissions-questions.html">A10</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Life-cycle emissions from mining, drilling, shipping and building plants, beyond the gas leaks counted here.</li>
<li>Methane from coal mines and oil wells, ozone, mercury, water and land.</li>
<li>How much electricity a tonne makes in a power plant: <a href="f04-power-plants.html">F4</a>.</li>
<li>Which CO₂ number answers which question: <a href="a10-emissions-questions.html">A10</a>.</li>
<li>Who pays for a city's plan, and how burden changes with it: Analyst lesson <a href="a13-fairness-jobs.html">A13</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: four myths, then four questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f11-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="coal" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Per tonne, coal sends more CO₂ into the air than any other fuel.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A tonne of oil makes 3.19 t and gas 2.69 t against coal's 2.44 t; per MWh of heat, coal's 341 kg is the most.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="scrubber" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A scrubber and a particle filter also cut a coal plant's CO₂.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. They cut SO₂ from 38 to 3.8 kg and fine particles from 5.2 to 0.4 kg a tonne, but the 2.44 t of CO₂ is unchanged.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="near" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A tall stack's pollution harms only the people who live next to it.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Nearby downwind communities can be heavily exposed, but in the spreading toy 74% of the exposure beyond 10 km happens more than 100 km away; EPA's estimates count harm across the continental United States.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bill" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A high energy burden means a high energy bill.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Prairie City's lowest-income group spends $1,940 a year, less than the highest group's $2,702, yet its burden is 14.9% against 1.9%.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f11">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="burden" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A household earns $30,000 a year and spends $2,100 on home energy. What is its energy burden?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">0.7%</li><li data-value="b">7.0%</li><li data-value="c">14%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>7.0%: 2,100 ÷ 30,000 = 0.070, above the 6% line ACEEE calls high.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="heat" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Per tonne, oil sends the most CO₂; per MWh of fuel heat, coal does. Why can both be true?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A tonne of coal gives much less heat</li><li data-value="b">Coal's controls add CO₂</li><li data-value="c">Oil's CO₂ is counted over 100 years</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A tonne of coal gives 7.2 MWh of heat against oil's 11.9 MWh, so each MWh of coal's heat carries more CO₂: 341 kg against 267.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="leak" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 2.3% leak adds about 0.70 t of CO₂e to a tonne of gas. About how much would a leak half as large add?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About 0.35 t</li><li data-value="b">About 0.70 t</li><li data-value="c">About 1.4 t</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 0.35 t: half the leak is about half the methane, so about half the CO₂e. The slider shows 0.33 t at 1.1% and 0.36 t at 1.2%.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dollars" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">With controls, EPA's estimate for a tonne of coal falls from about $3,130 to about $330. What do these dollars stand for?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The price of the coal</li><li data-value="b">Health harm, mostly early deaths</li><li data-value="c">What the controls cost</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Health harm: EPA's estimate, in 2019 dollars, of the early deaths and illness from the fine particles the tonne's pollution makes; an estimate, not a price.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>WHO counts 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019 from outdoor air pollution, and 99% of the world's people lived where its air quality guideline levels were not met.</p>
<p>ACEEE found 25% of U.S. households with a high energy burden and 13% with a severe one, using 2017 survey data.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Both are estimates with their own methods and dates; read the sources below before quoting them.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>IPCC (2006). <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/2006-ipcc-guidelines-for-national-greenhouse-gas-inventories/">2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories</a>, Volume 2 (Energy), Chapter 1: Table 1.2, p. 1.18 (net calorific values), Table 1.4, pp. 1.23–1.24 (CO₂ emission factors), section 1.4.1.2, p. 1.16 (net and gross heat).</li>
<li>Greenhouse Gas Protocol (2024). <a href="https://ghgprotocol.org/sites/default/files/2024-08/Global-Warming-Potential-Values%20%28August%202024%29.pdf">IPCC Global Warming Potential Values</a>, version 2.0, 7 August 2024: AR6 100-year values, p. 2; which methane value to use, p. 1.</li>
<li>Alvarez, R. A., et al. (2018). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aar7204">Assessment of methane emissions from the U.S. oil and gas supply chain</a>. Science 361, 186–188 (abstract).</li>
<li>Sherwin, E. D., et al. (2024). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07117-5">US oil and gas system emissions from nearly one million aerial site measurements</a>. Nature 627, 328–334 (abstract; campaign years from p. 329 and Fig. 2: 15 aerial campaigns, 2016 to 2021).</li>
<li>U.S. EPA. AP-42, Compilation of Air Pollutant Emission Factors: <a href="https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/documents/1.1_bituminous_and_subbituminous_coal_combustion.pdf">Section 1.1, Bituminous and Subbituminous Coal Combustion</a> (9/98), Tables 1.1-1, 1.1-3, 1.1-5 and 1.1-6; <a href="https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/documents/1.3_fuel_oil_combustion.pdf">Section 1.3, Fuel Oil Combustion</a> (5/10), Tables 1.3-1, 1.3-2 and 1.3-6; <a href="https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/documents/1.4_natural_gas_combustion.pdf">Section 1.4, Natural Gas Combustion</a> (revised 10/26), Tables 1.4-1 and 1.4-2; <a href="https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2020-11/documents/appa.pdf">Appendix A</a>, pp. A-5 and A-7 (read 6 November 2026).</li>
<li>U.S. EPA (2024). <a href="https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-06/source-apportionment-tsd-2024.pdf">Technical Support Document: Estimating the Benefit per Ton of Reducing Directly-Emitted PM2.5, PM2.5 Precursors and Ozone Precursors from 21 Sectors</a>. June 2024: Table 8, p. 22; method, p. 6.</li>
<li>World Health Organization (2024). Ambient (outdoor) air pollution, fact sheet, 24 October 2024 (read 6 November 2026).</li>
<li>ACEEE (2020). <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-05/Attachment%20J%20-%20ACEEE%2C%20How%20High%20are%20Household%20Energy%20Burdens.pdf">How High Are Household Energy Burdens?</a> September 2020 (copy on energy.gov).</li>
<li>U.S. Department of Energy. <a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/scep/low-income-energy-affordability-data-lead-tool">Low-Income Energy Affordability Data (LEAD) Tool</a>: definition of energy burden; 2018–2022 data (read 6 November 2026).</li>
<li>Prairie City's household groups: the course's shared city data (prairie-city.json), built from Census, BEA, EIA and DOE LEAD sources listed there.</li>
```
